title: Quantization Enables Private Dense Retrieval against Malicious Service Providers
abstract: Dense retrieval, the key component of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieves the most relevant documents by comparing dense vector representations of queries and passages from a large corpus. In privacy-sensitive applications, the server observes the query and controls which evidence is returned, creating both confidentiality and integrity risks. We formulate private dense retrieval as providing query privacy and retrieval integrity against a malicious server, and develop a two-round cryptographic protocol that provides both guarantees. Our protocol reduces private and verifiable retrieval to multiplication of a committed matrix by an encrypted vector and uses low-bit quantization to make this computation practical. We evaluate the resulting trade-off between cryptographic cost, retrieval quality, and downstream RAG accuracy across six embedding models, four language models, and corpora of up to 2.68 million passages. Our results show that, with a clipped quantizer, three-bit quantization largely preserves retrieval quality and downstream accuracy, while a private query over a corpus the size of a clinical reference requires one to three minutes of server time. These results suggest that private dense retrieval is already practical for moderately sized, privacy-sensitive corpora when minute-scale latency is acceptable.

title: An Intellectual Property Approach to the Use of Generative AI
abstract: The advent of many technologically powered inventions has not only made living easier but has aided the convenience of doing business in the digital age. Technological models like generative artificial intelligence, also known as generative AI, are now adopted by many businesses to stimulate their creative processes. Content generation has now been made easier as this is rapidly becoming the strength of the 21st-century business economy. As we enjoy the assistance rendered by generative artificial intelligence tools, we must address the concerns that emanate from this technology. One broad area that is worthy of note is the intellectual property concerns in the use of generative AI. This is pertinent to discuss because some of these AI models are trained on data that have, in recent times, been challenged due to the proprietary interest in such works. Also, the challenge that comes with determining the ownership of AIgenerated content, amongst other things, needs to be addressed. This research aims to give an exposition into the interface between these areas, discussing the conundrum that arises in this interface and proffering a balance to ensure mutual coexistence. The study found that as the world is moving and innovation is increasing, policies to balance this surge in innovation must be made proactively too. Legislative silence and dormancy will affect judicial capacity and that is not good for any country. The legal landscape must evolve to balance AI innovation with fair intellectual property protections. To achieve this, governments should prioritize the development of comprehensive legislation that addresses AI-generated content and its ownership. Additionally, collaboration between legal experts, technologists, and policymakers is essential to ensure laws remain adaptive and relevant as AI continues to evolve.

title: Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents
authors: Dr. L. Lakshmaiah, Dr. Raghu Kumar KS, Dr. S. Sunitha,Mr. Naveen Kumar Aakuthota.
abstract: developments in contemporary computing, transforming the way intelligent systems understand information, generate content, reason over knowledge, interact with users, and perform complex tasks. The rapid evolution of Large Language Models, multimodal foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation, intelligent agents, and autonomous workflows has created a new generation of AI systems that extend beyond conventional prediction and classification. These developments are influencing software engineering, scientific research, healthcare, education, business, robotics, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and many other domains. The book Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents has been developed to provide a comprehensive academic and engineering-oriented treatment of these emerging technologies. The book approaches Generative AI not merely as a collection of models or tools, but as an engineering discipline involving model architecture, data and knowledge integration, prompting, retrieval, agent orchestration, evaluation, security, deployment, optimization, and responsible operation. The objective is to provide readers with both conceptual foundations and a practical understanding of how modern Generative AI systems are designed and integrated into intelligent applications. The book begins with the foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models. Chapter 1, Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models, introduces the evolution of generative modeling from statistical Natural Language Processing to modern foundation models and LLMs. It examines the distinction between discriminative and generative learning and provides a detailed treatment of Transformer architecture, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, embeddings, and encoder–decoder architectures. The chapter further explores LLM pre-training, next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, tokenization, contextual representations, prompting, context engineering, inference optimization, quantization, and model ecosystems. Applications in intelligent tutoring, software engineering, healthcare, scientific knowledge discovery, business intelligence, and customer support establish the practical relevance of LLMs. Chapter 2, LLM Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Multimodal Intelligence, moves from model fundamentals toward application engineering. It explains how LLM APIs, model-serving architectures, prompt templates, structured outputs, function calling, and schema-constrained generation can be integrated into production applications. Particular emphasis is given to Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, grounding, and knowledge-intensive generation. Advanced retrieval techniques such as hybrid search, dense retrieval, query expansion, query decomposition, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval are examined. The chapter also discusses vector databases, metadata filtering, knowledge graphs, multimodal foundation models, multimodal embeddings, fine-tuning, LoRA, continual adaptation, orchestration frameworks, memory management, and production-oriented architectures. Applications in enterprise knowledge systems, healthcare, scientific research, legal and financial analysis, education, manufacturing, and intelligent search demonstrate the breadth of these technologies. Chapter 3, Intelligent Agents and Agentic AI Engineering, examines the transition from prompt-driven systems to goal-oriented and autonomous AI agents. It introduces reactive, deliberative, and hybrid agent architectures and explains how perception, reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and action contribute to intelligent behavior. The chapter explores task decomposition, reasoning strategies, reflection, self-correction, decision-making, function calling, external APIs, code execution, search tools, databases, and computational tools. Particular attention is given to short-term and long-term memory, episodic and semantic memory, context compression, persistent memory, and multi-agent collaboration. Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation and autonomous knowledge acquisition are introduced as important mechanisms for developing research-oriented and knowledge-intensive agents. The chapter concludes with agent evaluation, reliability, observability, trajectory analysis, tool-use accuracy, failure analysis, and applications in autonomous software engineering, research, customer service, healthcare, education, finance, and enterprise automation. As Generative AI systems become increasingly capable, their reliability, security, privacy, and responsible deployment become essential. Chapter 4, Secure, Responsible, and Production-Ready Generative AI Engineering, addresses these requirements. It introduces systematic approaches to LLM and application evaluation, benchmarking, human evaluation, automated evaluation, and task-specific assessment. The chapter examines hallucination, factuality, grounded generation, fact verification, confidence estimation, and uncertainty-aware generation. Security topics include prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, model security, and agent security. Privacy-preserving Generative AI is explored through sensitive-data protection, anonymization, federated learning, and privacy-preserving retrieval and inference. The chapter further addresses fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, human oversight, governance, and responsible deployment. Production engineering topics include LLMOps, MLOps, model lifecycle management, prompt and model versioning, monitoring, observability, continuous evaluation, deployment, distributed inference, quantization, distillation, accelerator optimization, and edge AI. Chapter 5, Emerging Trends and Advanced Applications of Generative AI, looks toward the future of the field. It examines reasoning-centric AI models, test-time computation, self-reflection, verification, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and hybrid intelligence. Agentic AI and autonomous workflows are explored through autonomous task execution, human–agent collaboration, workflow automation, and self-improving agent architectures. The chapter also examines Generative AI for software engineering, including coding assistants, automated debugging, software testing, vulnerability detection, and autonomous development agents. Applications in scientific discovery, drug and material design, engineering optimization, clinical decision support, robotics, and embodied intelligence demonstrate the expanding role of Generative AI in the physical and scientific world. The chapter further examines Small Language Models, edge AI, on-device inference, domain-specific foundation models, and energy-efficient Generative AI. Future architectures involving multimodal foundation models, world models, persistent AI memory, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems are discussed as important directions for next-generation intelligent systems. Finally, emerging applications such as autonomous organizations, personalized education, smart cities, intelligent infrastructure, digital twins, industrial AI, and next-generation human–AI collaboration illustrate the broader societal and technological implications of Generative AI. The engineering lifecycle can therefore be summarized as: Understand → Design → Generate → Retrieve → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Secure → Deploy → Monitor → Improve The book also emphasizes the distinction between generating a plausible output and producing a reliable result. Generative AI systems can produce highly fluent responses while still containing factual errors, unsupported assumptions, security vulnerabilities, or inappropriate recommendations. Consequently, validation, grounding, evaluation, human oversight, and responsible deployment are treated as fundamental engineering requirements rather than optional additions. Another important objective of the book is to establish a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical system development. Students and professionals need to understand not only how Transformers and LLMs work, but also how these models are incorporated into real applications through APIs, vector databases, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, agents, tools, memory systems, and deployment platforms. The book therefore follows a progressive structure that moves from foundations to application engineering, from application engineering to intelligent agents, from agents to secure production systems, and finally toward emerging architectures and advanced applications. The book is intended for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and related disciplines. It is also designed to support researchers, educators, software engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals, and readers who wish to develop a systematic understanding of Generative AI engineering. The material can be used for university courses, advanced electives, professional training programs, research preparation, and self-directed learning. The ultimate objective of Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents is to help readers move from simply using Generative AI tools toward understanding, designing, evaluating, and engineering intelligent systems. Generative AI is becoming an important component of modern computing infrastructure, and its future will depend not only on increasingly capable models but also on the ability to build systems that are reliable, secure, efficient, explainable, scalable, responsible, and human-centered. Chapter 1, Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models, introduces the evolution of generative modeling from statistical Natural Language Processing to modern foundation models and LLMs. It examines the distinction between discriminative and generative learning and provides a detailed treatment of Transformer architecture, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, embeddings, and encoder–decoder architectures. The chapter further explores LLM pre-training, next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, tokenization, contextual representations, prompting, context engineering, inference optimization, quantization, and model ecosystems. Applications in intelligent tutoring, software engineering, healthcare, scientific knowledge discovery, business intelligence, and customer support establish the practical relevance of LLMs. Chapter 2, LLM Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Multimodal Intelligence, moves from model fundamentals toward application engineering. It explains how LLM APIs, model-serving architectures, prompt templates, structured outputs, function calling, and schema-constrained generation can be integrated into production applications. Particular emphasis is given to Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, grounding, and knowledge-intensive generation. Advanced retrieval techniques such as hybrid search, dense retrieval, query expansion, query decomposition, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval are examined. The chapter also discusses vector databases, metadata filtering, knowledge graphs, multimodal foundation models, multimodal embeddings, fine-tuning, LoRA, continual adaptation, orchestration frameworks, memory management, and production-oriented architectures. Applications in enterprise knowledge systems, healthcare, scientific research, legal and financial analysis, education, manufacturing, and intelligent search demonstrate the breadth of these technologies. Chapter 3, Intelligent Agents and Agentic AI Engineering, examines the transition from prompt-driven systems to goal-oriented and autonomous AI agents. It introduces reactive, deliberative, and hybrid agent architectures and explains how perception, reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and action contribute to intelligent behavior. The chapter explores task decomposition, reasoning strategies, reflection, self-correction, decision-making, function calling, external APIs, code execution, search tools, databases, and computational tools. Particular attention is given to short-term and long-term memory, episodic and semantic memory, context compression, persistent memory, and multi-agent collaboration. Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation and autonomous knowledge acquisition are introduced as important mechanisms for developing research-oriented and knowledge-intensive agents. The chapter concludes with agent evaluation, reliability, observability, trajectory analysis, tool-use accuracy, failure analysis, and applications in autonomous software engineering, research, customer service, healthcare, education, finance, and enterprise automation. As Generative AI systems become increasingly capable, their reliability, security, privacy, and responsible deployment become essential. Chapter 4, Secure, Responsible, and Production-Ready Generative AI Engineering, addresses these requirements. It introduces systematic approaches to LLM and application evaluation, benchmarking, human evaluation, automated evaluation, and task-specific assessment. The chapter examines hallucination, factuality, grounded generation, fact verification, confidence estimation, and uncertainty-aware generation. Security topics include prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, model security, and agent security. Privacy-preserving Generative AI is explored through sensitive-data protection, anonymization, federated learning, and privacy-preserving retrieval and inference. The chapter further addresses fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, human oversight, governance, and responsible deployment. Production engineering topics include LLMOps, MLOps, model lifecycle management, prompt and model versioning, monitoring, observability, continuous evaluation, deployment, distributed inference, quantization, distillation, accelerator optimization, and edge AI. Chapter 5, Emerging Trends and Advanced Applications of Generative AI, looks toward the future of the field. It examines reasoning-centric AI models, test-time computation, self-reflection, verification, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and hybrid intelligence. Agentic AI and autonomous workflows are explored through autonomous task execution, human–agent collaboration, workflow automation, and self-improving agent architectures. The chapter also examines Generative AI for software engineering, including coding assistants, automated debugging, software testing, vulnerability detection, and autonomous development agents. Applications in scientific discovery, drug and material design, engineering optimization, clinical decision support, robotics, and embodied intelligence demonstrate the expanding role of Generative AI in the physical and scientific world. The chapter further examines Small Language Models, edge AI, on-device inference, domain-specific foundation models, and energy-efficient Generative AI. Future architectures involving multimodal foundation models, world models, persistent AI memory, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems are discussed as important directions for next-generation intelligent systems. Finally, emerging applications such as autonomous organizations, personalized education, smart cities, intelligent infrastructure, digital twins, industrial AI, and next-generation human–AI collaboration illustrate the broader societal and technological implications of Generative AI. The engineering lifecycle can therefore be summarized as: Understand → Design → Generate → Retrieve → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Secure → Deploy → Monitor → Improve The book also emphasizes the distinction between generating a plausible output and producing a reliable result. Generative AI systems can produce highly fluent responses while still containing factual errors, unsupported assumptions, security vulnerabilities, or inappropriate recommendations. Consequently, validation, grounding, evaluation, human oversight, and responsible deployment are treated as fundamental engineering requirements rather than optional additions. Another important objective of the book is to establish a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical system development. Students and professionals need to understand not only how Transformers and LLMs work, but also how these models are incorporated into real applications through APIs, vector databases, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, agents, tools, memory systems, and deployment platforms. The book therefore follows a progressive structure that moves from foundations to application engineering, from application engineering to intelligent agents, from agents to secure production systems, and finally toward emerging architectures and advanced applications. The book is intended for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and related disciplines. It is also designed to support researchers, educators, software engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals, and readers who wish to develop a systematic understanding of Generative AI engineering. The material can be used for university courses, advanced electives, professional training programs, research preparation, and self-directed learning. title: For a Function That Is Not Convex, Where You Start Decides the Answer ── f(x)=x^4-3x^2+0.5x has a left minimum at -1.264459 (f=-2.872457) and a right minimum at 1.180734 (f=-1.648425), with a maximum between at 0.083725 ── the separator is whether the second derivative is positive everywhere or negative somewhere ── [Paper 771]
abstract: Gradient descent seeks a minimum by walking downhill. If the landscape is a single valley, every start reaches the same bottom. When there are two valleys, how much the start decides the destination is counted. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──that local minima of convex functions are global, that for non-convex functions the destination of gradient descent is set by the basin of attraction of the start, and that the basin boundary is a maximum are all known (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, Nocedal and Wright 2006). One dimension──only functions of one variable are considered; multidimensional landscapes with saddles are not treated. One method──only plain gradient descent with step 0.01 is used; stochastic methods, momentum and divergence at large steps are not treated. Uniform starts──1001 equally spaced points on [-2,2] are the starts. No real problem is claimed──particular learning or optimisation problems are not treated. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 734 showed that what caps the step size is not the size of the gradient but the curvature in the steepest direction──its scope note stated that it was limited to quadratic functions and would not treat non-convex surfaces or saddles. There every start reached the same point. Here, on a non-convex surface, nearly half the starts reach a bottom that is not the global minimum. Paper 507 is also cited──there a convex function returned to itself after two transforms. Here a convex function sends every start to one point, and a non-convex one lets the start split the answer. What is added is tabulating stationary points with the signs of their second derivatives, counting the destinations of 1001 starts and checking them against the position of the maximum, showing that for a convex function the spread stays at 1.027x10^-15, and placing the separator on whether the second derivative turns negative somewhere. First, a non-convex function has two bottoms──a left minimum at -1.264459 and a right minimum at 1.180734, with a maximum at 0.083725 between (Section 2). Second, the two bottoms differ in depth──f is -2.872457 on the left and -1.648425 on the right; the global minimum is on the left (Section 2). Third, and this is the core. The start splits the destination, and nearly half reach the shallower bottom──of 1001 starts, a share 0.520480 goes left and 0.479520 right (Section 3). Fourth, the boundary is set by the position of the maximum──the formula gives 0.520931, differing from the grid share by 0.000452 (Section 3). Fifth, if convex, the start does not matter──all 1001 points reach -0.226699, with a spread of 1.027x10^-15 (Section 3). Sixth, the separator is whether the second derivative is positive everywhere or negative somewhere──"the minimum was found by gradient descent" does not say which minimum until one says whether the function is convex (Section 4). For a function that is not convex, where you start decides the answer. f(x)=x^4-3x^2+0.5x has a left minimum at -1.264459 (f=-2.872457) and a right minimum at 1.180734 (f=-1.648425), with a maximum at 0.083725 between──the global minimum is on the left. Descending from 1001 points on [-2,2] splits them 0.520480 left and 0.479520 right, so nearly half reach the shallower bottom; the boundary is set by the maximum, the formula share 0.520931 differing from the grid by 0.000452──gradient descent does not know which bottom is deeper. For the convex x^4+x^2+0.5x all 1001 points reached -0.226699, with a spread of 1.027x10^-15. The separator is whether the second derivative is positive everywhere or negative somewhere──"the minimum was found by gradient descent" does not say which minimum until one says whether the function is convex. Placed among the earlier papers──Paper 734 kept to quadratics and set non-convex surfaces aside; this counts, beyond that, the start splitting the destination. To be honest──only one-dimensional functions are considered, with no saddles, stochastic methods or real problems. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. Keywords: convexity, local minimum, gradient descent, dependence on the start, basin of attraction, global minimum. ----- 勾配降下は、坂を下って最小を探す。坂が一つの谷なら、どこから下りても同じ底に着く。谷が二つあるとき、始点が行き先をどれだけ決めるかを数える。新しい定理も法則も主張しない。 本稿の射程(射程注記):新しい定理も法則も主張しない──凸関数では局所最小が大域最小であること、凸でない関数では勾配降下の行き先が始点の引き込み領域で決まること、その境が極大であることは、いずれも既知である(ボイド&ヴァンデンベルグ 2004、ノセダル&ライト 2006)。一次元に限る──一変数の関数だけを見て、鞍点のある多次元の面は扱わない。手法を限る──刻み 0.01 の素朴な勾配降下だけを使い、確率的な方法、運動量、大きな刻みでの発散は扱わない。始点を一様に置く──[-2,2] に等間隔に置いた 1001 点を始点とする。実在の問題を主張しない──個別の学習問題や最適化問題は扱わない。既刊との関係:論文734 は、歩幅の天井を決めているのが勾配の大きさではなく、いちばん急な向きの曲率であることを示した──その射程注記は「二次関数に限る──非凸な面、鞍点…は扱わない」と明記していた。そこではどこから始めても同じ一点に着いた。ここでは凸でない面の上で、始点のほぼ半分が大域の最小でない底に着く。論文507 も引く──そこでは凸関数なら変換を二回して元に戻った。ここでは凸なら始点に依らず一点に着き、凸でなければ始点が答を分ける。加えたのは、停留点と二階微分の符号を並べたこと、1001 の始点の行き先を数え、極大の位置の式と照らしたこと、凸な関数でばらつきが 1.027x10^-15 に収まることを示したこと、分離子を「二階微分が負になるところがあるか」に置いたことである。 第一に、凸でない関数には、底が二つある──左の極小 -1.264459 と右の極小 1.180734、あいだに極大 0.083725(第2節)。 第二に、二つの底の深さは違う──f は左で -2.872457、右で -1.648425 で、大域の最小は左(第2節)。 第三に、これが本稿の芯である。始点が行き先を分け、ほぼ半分が浅い底に着く──1001 点のうち左へ 0.520480、右へ 0.479520(第3節)。 第四に、境を決めているのは極大の位置である──式の割合 0.520931 と、格子の割合との差は 0.000452(第3節)。 第五に、凸なら、始点は答に効かない──1001 点すべてが -0.226699 に着き、ばらつきは 1.027x10^-15(第3節)。 第六に、分離子は、二階微分がどこでも正か、負になるところがあるかである──「勾配降下で最小を求めた」は、関数が凸かを言うまで、どの最小かが決まらない(第4節)。 凸でない関数では、どこから始めたかが答を決める。 f(x)=x^4-3x^2+0.5x には左の極小 -1.264459(f=-2.872457)と右の極小 1.180734(f=-1.648425)があり、あいだに極大 0.083725 が立つ──大域の最小は左である。[-2,2] の 1001 点から勾配降下すると、左へ 0.520480、右へ 0.479520 に分かれ、始点のほぼ半分が浅い底に着く。境は極大の位置が決め、式の割合 0.520931 と格子の差は 0.000452 だった──勾配降下は、どちらの底が深いかを知らない。凸な x^4+x^2+0.5x では 1001 点すべてが -0.226699 に着き、ばらつきは 1.027x10^-15 だった。分離子は、二階微分がどこでも正か、負になるところがあるかである──「勾配降下で最小を求めた」は、関数が凸かを言うまで、どの最小かが決まらない。既刊との位置──論文734 は二次関数に限り非凸な面を扱わないと明記した。ここはその外で、始点が行き先を分けることを数えた。正直に言えば──一次元の関数だけで、鞍点も確率的な方法も実在の問題も扱っていない。 作成にあたって:本稿の着想と内容は、著者自身の考察に基づくものです。文章の構成整理や英訳、数式の確認には AI(大規模言語モデル)の助力を得ました。最終的な内容の解釈や誤りがあれば、それらはすべて著者の責に帰します。お気づきの点があれば、ご教示いただければ幸いです。 キーワード:凸性、局所最小、勾配降下、初期値依存、引き込み領域、大域最小。

title: ICNN-Bi-LSTM framework for lung cancer classification in CT imaging with statistical and texture pattern extractors
abstract: Abstract One of the deadliest and most terrible diseases in the world is lung cancer; however, prompt analysis and care may safeguard lives. When a person with lung cancer does not exhibit early symptoms, it is very challenging to determine and predict the affected area. Despite being the most effective imaging method in the medical sector, CT scan images are more challenging for physicians to interpret and diagnose diseases. Consequently, computer-aided diagnostics can be useful in helping medical professionals to precisely detect cancer cells. This research introduces a new lung cancer classification (LCC) model. The initial pre-processing is performed with Adaptive Weiner Filtering (AWF), followed by Modified Deep joint (DJ) Segmentation, which is processed to segment the ROI and non-ROI regions. Then, Local Gradient Increasing Pattern (LGIP), Median Binary Pattern (MBP), Multi-texton (MT) features, and Statistical features are extracted. Then, classification is done using HC that involves an Improved Convolutional Neural Network (Imp CNN) and Bi-LSTM models. Finally, investigation outcomes on wide-ranging metrics show the performance of the proposed model. The proposed LCC model achieves higher classification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art lung cancer classification approaches, confirming its superiority and effectiveness.

Despite being the most effective imaging method in the medical sector, CT scan images are more challenging for physicians to interpret and diagnose diseases. Consequently, computer-aided diagnostics can be useful in helping medical professionals to precisely detect cancer cells. This research introduces a new lung cancer classification (LCC) model. The initial pre-processing is performed with Adaptive Weiner Filtering (AWF), followed by Modified Deep joint (DJ) Segmentation, which is processed to segment the ROI and non-ROI regions. Then, Local Gradient Increasing Pattern (LGIP), Median Binary Pattern (MBP), Multi-texton (MT) features, and Statistical features are extracted. Then, classification is done using HC that involves an Improved Convolutional Neural Network (Imp CNN) and Bi-LSTM models. Finally, investigation outcomes on wide-ranging metrics show the performance of the proposed model. The proposed LCC model achieves higher classification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art lung cancer classification approaches, confirming its superiority and effectiveness.

title: GeoWind2Plan: Mission-Time 3D Urban Wind Prediction for Energy-Efficient UAV Planning
abstract: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, making unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) energy depend on local wind exposure as well as path length. However, building-resolved wind information is rarely available when a mission must be planned. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can produce high-fidelity urban flow fields, but each simulation is tied to a fixed inflow boundary condition and can take hours to days, which is incompatible with urban UAV missions that typically last minutes to tens of minutes. We present GeoWind2Plan, a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework for mission-time 3D urban wind prediction and energy-efficient UAV planning. Given only a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan transforms the building geometry into a reference-wind frame, predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches with a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, stitches them into a queryable local wind field, and optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. Rather than pursuing CFD-perfect reconstruction, GeoWind2Plan targets decision-useful wind prediction: trajectories are planned with predicted wind and evaluated under high-fidelity CFD wind. Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, GeoWind2Plan performs corridor-localized wind inference in about 3 seconds, compared with roughly 8 hours for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time.

title: Learning to Act under Visual Interruptions with Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, but they are typically developed and evaluated with all camera streams available throughout task execution. When a camera stops delivering frames during task execution, the policy must continue acting without access to subsequent observations from the missing view. Despite its practical importance, how such interruptions affect closed-loop manipulation remains insufficiently understood. To investigate this problem, we introduce MAIL-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates visual interruptions with VLA models. By interrupting different cameras at multiple stages of each policy's successful reference trajectory, MAIL-Bench measures how well policies retain their capabilities when visual inputs become unavailable. Building on this benchmark, we propose MINT, which first trains VLA policies to remain functional under missing visual inputs. At inference time, MINT selectively supplements missing observations using optical-flow extrapolation or an action-conditioned world model, and withdraws predicted views when they become unreliable. Experiments on π_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5 show that MINT significantly improves task success under camera loss over the original models. Experiments on AgiBot G2 further demonstrate the real-robot deployment under camera loss. The benchmark is available at https://minglejiang.github.io/Mail-Bench/

title: EOPSA: Efficient On-Policy Self-Distilled Safety Alignment
abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for safety alignment, delivering dense, token-level supervision by distilling from a teacher conditioned on refusal-oriented privileged prompts. However, we reveal that this paradigm suffers from critical inefficiencies that degrade both training efficiency and general reasoning capabilities. Specifically, we diagnose two fundamental bottlenecks: (1) supervisory collapse over extended rollouts, where the teacher's corrective efficacy degrades precipitously as the student's generation prefix lengthens, injecting noisy gradients into late-stage tokens; and (2) gradient dilution from stylistic shifts, where the distillation objective is dominated by safety-irrelevant stylistic discrepancies induced by privileged prompting, washing out genuine safety signals and impairing base reasoning. To resolve these issues, we propose Efficient On-Policy Self-Distilled Safety Alignment (EOPSA), which concentrates computational and gradient budgets exclusively on reliably supervised, safety-critical tokens. EOPSA incorporates two coordinated mechanisms: (i) Adaptive Rollout Scheduling, which dynamically bounds the generation horizon guided by a novel Teacher Rescue Rate (TRR) metric to operate strictly within reliable supervision regimes; and (ii) Selective Distillation, which filters out safety-neutral tokens to restrict gradient updates exclusively to safety-pivotal transitions. Extensive evaluations across reasoning models up to 32B parameters demonstrate that EOPSA slashes rollout computation by $\sim$50% and backpropagates through merely $\sim$2% of tokens, consistently outperforming full-token distillation baselines in both safety compliance and reasoning retention.

title: SPACE-LoRA: Allocating Activation-Subspace Protection for Continual Learning
abstract: This study addresses the catastrophic forgetting problem that occurs when sequentially learning successive tasks using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) from a lifelong learning perspective. While existing approaches have primarily constrained parameter updates or learning subspaces to reduce interference with past knowledge, they have not fully considered additive interference. This occurs when a newly added residual adapter on top of a fixed past model generates non-zero responses along input directions important for old tasks, thereby altering previous predictions. To this end, we propose Subspace Protection with Allocated Capacity for Efficient Continual Adaptation (SPACE-LoRA). SPACE-LoRA directly suppresses the responses of the new residual branch along input activation directions that are important for old tasks and adaptively determines the protection coverage for each module based on past-task sensitivity estimated via a common Fisher sensitivity-based coverage target. Under a fixed LoRA rank, this approach adaptively adjusts module-specific protection coverage while suppressing interference along input directions sensitive to old tasks. We assess the effectiveness of activation-subspace protection in mitigating catastrophic forgetting and examine the role of sensitivity-guided protection in continual learning across diverse tasks. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SPACE-LoRA-7864.

title: DreamingGoose: Staged Distillation from Autoregressive Transformers to Bidirectional Recurrent Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Pretrained autoregressive Transformers represent a large sunk investment in compute. Existing conversion methods reuse that investment by changing either the architecture (attention to recurrence) or the objective (next-token prediction to denoising), never both. We convert Qwen3 teachers at 1.7B and 8B into attention-free, bidirectional, gated-delta-rule diffusion students in three stages, so that each capability can be traced to the stage that kept or lost it. Language modeling transfers only partially and in-distribution; in-context retrieval does not transfer. On a multi-query recall probe where the teachers score 0.34-0.58, both converted students score 0.000, and diffusion pretraining alone does not restore retrieval. A retrieval curriculum in the final stage, which gradually lengthens the gap between a key-value table and the queries that address it, restores it only stochastically: on a fixed schedule, one seed in three learns to retrieve. Advancing the gap only while a running accuracy estimate stays above a threshold works for all three of those seeds, holds on real text, and carries unchanged to 8B, where two of three seeds succeed. The third had not learned within its fixed 16k-step budget: retrieval switches on abruptly at a seed-dependent step (6.5k and 11k in the other two), so a fixed budget can cut a late run off. One boundary survives every intervention: every model that learns retrieval scores 0.000 on tokens that never appeared in a retrieval episode, and an arm that resamples the key and value tokens every batch shows this is a coverage limit, not memorization of particular bindings. Separately, we convert a 7B code model into a 3:1 recurrent-attention block-diffusion hybrid over 85k steps and report two negative training results.

title: MAS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) split a task across specialized roles and are promising on complex tasks, yet a prevailing approach relies on inference-time orchestration alone. General-purpose APIs are costly and hard to customize, while small models with role prompts rarely develop stable role competence or reliable collaboration, so post-training a MAS jointly is central. Most attempts use reinforcement learning, whose team-level reward leaves undetermined which step of which agent brought about the outcome, while local rewards need redesigning per task. On-policy distillation (OPD) gives token-level teacher supervision on trajectories the student samples, a denser signal needing no local reward, yet is underexplored for the interdependent agents of a MAS. Two difficulties arise: building complementary specialization from a judgement of which role a behavior belongs to while preserving the knowledge all roles need, and turning cross-agent collaborative information into supervision OPD can exploit. We present MAS-OPD, where Role-Advantage Specialization defines the role advantage as the difference between the teacher signals under target and non-target role conditions, and Privileged Attribution for Coordination attributes an interaction conflict to its source and supplies it to the teacher alone as privileged information. Extensive experiments on code and mathematics benchmarks show that MAS-OPD attains the highest mean score at both student scales and leads the agents to develop clearer role specialization and more effective collaborative behavior.

title: CASS: Contribution-Aware Structured Sparsity for Model Merging
abstract: Model merging integrates task-specific fine-tuned models into a single multi-task model, but often suffers from parameter interference caused by conflicting task-vector updates. Existing methods typically mitigate conflicts by pruning task vectors based on weight magnitude or random heuristics, treating Transformers as unstructured ``bags of parameters'' and overlooking their inherent modularity. In this paper, we propose \textbf{C}ontribution-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{S}tructured \textbf{S}parsity (CASS), a unified framework that reduces parameter interference by identifying and preserving task-specific components. At the core of CASS is a contribution-aware structured mask that identifies task-relevant attention heads and FFN neurons. We instantiate this mask in two settings: CASS-Merging, the primary post-hoc setting where masks serve as a plug-and-play denoising filter for existing merging operators, and CASS-Tuning, an extension for scenarios with fine-tuning access where masks constrain gradients to reduce structural overlap between task vectors. Our analysis shows that task-relevant components are sparse and partially disjoint, supporting structured component-level filtering as an effective way to reduce merging interference. Extensive experiments across vision (ViT, 20 tasks) and language (RoBERTa, 8 tasks; Qwen2.5, 4 tasks) benchmarks demonstrate that CASS improves a range of representative merging baselines.

title: Vision--Language Signals in Constrained RL: Safety Gains Without Anticipation
abstract: Safe reinforcement learning seeks policies that maximise task performance while satisfying safety constraints. In driving benchmarks, however, collision costs typically appear only at the time of collision, providing no advance warning of an approaching hazard. Frozen vision--language models can provide dense semantic feedback, yet it remains unclear whether their scores anticipate collisions and which component drives an observed safety improvement. Episodic cost can also favour policies that make little task progress. To address these gaps, we propose VLM-Safe-RL, a framework that integrates frozen CLIP signals into PPO-Lagrangian through reward shaping and an augmented multiplier update. On MetaDrive Hard, which combines the densest traffic with the largest map, the catastrophe rate falls from 31.6\% to 19.4\%. FormulaOne-L2 analysis finds no evidence that the CLIP signals anticipate collisions and shows that the VLM term has a negligible effect on the Lagrange multiplier. These findings show a conditional reduction in observed catastrophe rate without evidence of collision anticipation.

title: LEGO-Anything: Coding Agents for 3D Scene Reconstruction
abstract: A 3D scene reconstructed from a single image is most useful when represented not as a rendering or a fixed 3D output, but as an explicit scene program whose execution yields a scene that can be inspected, edited, and queried. We present LEGO-Anything, an Image-to-Code framework in which a coding agent iteratively writes and executes Blender code, inspects scenes and renderings, and revises the program. To evaluate end-to-end scene recovery, we introduce LEGO-Bench, a simulator-grounded benchmark with 208 images from 104 diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. LEGO-Bench separately scores artifact validity, visible-surface geometry, and rendered appearance. Its simulator-grounded design enables extensibility and precise automatic evaluation. Among evaluated agents, GPT-6-astra achieves the strongest overall results, with 53.4% indoor and 39.6% outdoor scores, yet substantial gaps remain between delivering valid scene artifacts and faithfully recovering scene geometry and appearance. Analysis of agent construction trajectories reveals three recurring issues: weak scene initialization, regressive edits during iteration, and unreliable self-evaluation. These findings motivate LEGO-Plugin, a training-free harness plugin for more controlled iterative scene construction, which improves all six evaluated models, with relative gains of up to 62.7% in overall score. Finally, we test whether reconstructed scenes can represent natural images and support vision tasks. In LEGO-World, we derive object detections, instance masks, and relative depth as deterministic queries on scenes reconstructed by GPT-6-astra. These readouts show non-trivial performance across all three tasks but fall well short of specialized vision models, suggesting that program-constructed scenes from current coding agents are a promising but not yet sufficiently precise representation of natural images.

title: What Makes World Action Models Generalize? An Empirical Study of Test-Time Future Modeling
abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the future alongside actions during training. Due to the heavy computation cost of video denoising, whether the future must still be generated during inference is disputed: Explicit WAMs denoise it into clean frames along with every action chunk, whereas Latent WAMs discard it entirely for acceleration. We find that latent WAMs, despite matching explicit ones on in-distribution tasks, fail to retain the generalization benefits that originally motivated WAMs. To demonstrate this, we evaluate generalization along three axes: environmental perturbation, data efficiency, and task generalization. Controlled comparisons with a matched backbone, training data, and budget reveal consistent degradation across all three axes when the action expert no longer conditions on future representations. Further analysis shows that the gap arises almost entirely from the first denoising step: the benefit comes from preparing the future, not generating it. We therefore propose Simple-WAM, which simplifies future modeling into a single forward pass of fully noised video tokens and adapts the training-time noise schedule to this inference behavior. Across simulation and real-world tasks, Simple-WAM achieves the best of both worlds, leading explicit WAMs in generalization performance with efficiency comparable to Latent WAMs. Project Page: https://zrporz.github.io/Simple-WAM-Web/

title: The Huffman Code Is Optimal, but Only Within the Constraint That Code Lengths Be Whole Numbers ── With probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8 the average length 1.750000 meets the entropy 1.750000 exactly ── the separator is whether each symbol's probability is a power of 2 ── [Paper 752]
abstract: The Huffman code is known as the code of shortest average length. That optimality does not mean reaching the entropy. Optimal within what, and how far short, is counted. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──that the Huffman code minimises average length among prefix codes, that average length lies at least at the entropy and below entropy plus 1, that grouping brings the gap below 1/k, and the Kraft inequality are all known (Huffman 1952, Cover and Thomas 2006). Codes without the whole-number constraint are not treated──schemes such as arithmetic coding, which give symbols fractional lengths, are only named. The source is limited──only memoryless two- and four-symbol sources with known probabilities are considered. Cost is not treated──the exponential growth of the code table with grouping, and delay, are not treated. No real data are claimed──particular files and compressors are not treated. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 304 showed that channel capacity is attained at no finite code length and that the loss falls only as 1/sqrt(n)──its scope note stated that which codes approach capacity would not be treated at all. This is the noiseless source side: the entropy is met exactly symbol by symbol when probabilities are powers of 2, and otherwise approached within 1/k. Whether it is reached at finite length is decided by the form of the probabilities. Paper 163 is also cited──it separated "a good code exists" from "here is a good code". Huffman is on the "here is" side, a construction shown optimal within whole-number lengths. What is added is confirming exact arrival for powers of 2, showing that for two skewed symbols the "optimal code" spends 12.377289 times the entropy, tabulating the gap, 1/k and the Kraft sum for each grouping, and placing the separator on whether probabilities are powers of 2. First, with probabilities that are powers of 2, it arrives exactly──1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8: average length 1.750000, entropy 1.750000 (Section 2). Second, for two skewed symbols, the optimal code is far off──at probability 0.99 the entropy is 0.080793 bits, while symbol-by-symbol Huffman spends 1.000000 bit (Section 3). Third, and this is the core. The "optimal code" spends 12.377289 times the entropy──because lengths must be whole numbers and no symbol can be given less than 1 bit (Section 3). Fourth, grouping approaches, but only from above──groups of 2, 4 and 8 give 0.514950, 0.272698 and 0.157158 bits, always within 1/k (Section 3). Fifth, even at 8, still 1.945193 times──every Kraft sum is 1.000000, so the code has no gaps (Section 3). Sixth, the separator is whether each symbol's probability is a power of 2──if so, symbol-by-symbol coding arrives; if not, the gap shrinks with grouping but never vanishes (Section 4). The Huffman code is optimal, but only within the constraint that code lengths be whole numbers. With probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8 the average length 1.750000 meets the entropy 1.750000 exactly──because the lengths are -log_2p_i themselves. But for two symbols with one at probability 0.99, against an entropy of 0.080793 bits symbol-by-symbol Huffman spends 1.000000 bit, 12.377289 times the entropy──no symbol can be given less than 1 bit. Grouping 2, 4 and 8 symbols brings it to 0.514950, 0.272698 and 0.157158 bits, always within 1/k, yet at 8 still 1.945193 times the entropy. The separator is whether each symbol's probability is a power of 2──"is Huffman optimal?" has no answer until one says optimal within what, and what form the probabilities take. Placed among the earlier papers──Paper 304 showed channel capacity unreached at finite length; on the source side, whether the limit is reached at finite length depends on the probabilities. On the "here is" side of Paper 163 stands a conditional optimum. To be honest──arithmetic coding, sources with memory and table size are not treated. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. Keywords: Huffman code, entropy, code length, Kraft inequality, coding symbols in groups, whole-number constraint. ----- ハフマン符号は、平均の長さが最も短い符号として知られる。けれど、その最適はエントロピーに届くことを意味しない。何の中での最適かと、どれだけ届かないかを数える。新しい定理も法則も主張しない。 本稿の射程(射程注記):新しい定理も法則も主張しない──ハフマン符号が語頭符号の中で平均の長さを最小にすること、平均の長さがエントロピー以上・エントロピー+1 未満であること、記号をまとめると差が 1/k 未満になること、クラフトの不等式は、いずれも既知である(ハフマン 1952、カバー&トーマス 2006)。整数の縛りの無い符号を扱わない──算術符号のように一記号に端数の長さを割り当てる方式は、名前を挙げるにとどめる。情報源を限る──記憶の無い、確率の分かっている二記号と四記号の情報源だけを見る。手間を扱わない──まとめると符号表が指数で大きくなることや、遅延は扱わない。実在のデータを主張しない──個別のファイルや圧縮器の性能は扱わない。既刊との関係:論文304 は、通信路容量がどの有限の符号長でも達成されず、損失が 1/sqrt(n) でしか減らないことを示した──その射程注記は、どの符号が容量に近づくかは一切扱わないと明記していた。ここは雑音の無い情報源の側で、エントロピーは確率が 2 の冪なら一記号ずつでちょうど届き、そうでなければ差が 1/k 未満で近づく。有限で届くかどうかが、確率の形で決まる。論文163 も引く──そこでは「良い符号が在る」と「これが良い符号だ」を分けた。ハフマンは「これだ」の側で、しかも整数の長さの中で最適と示される構成である。加えたのは、2 の冪でちょうど届くことを確かめたこと、偏った二記号で「最適な符号」が 12.377289 倍を使うことを示したこと、まとめる長さごとに差と 1/k とクラフト和を並べたこと、分離子を「確率が 2 の冪か」に置いたことである。 第一に、確率が 2 の冪なら、ちょうど届く──1/2・1/4・1/8・1/8 で平均の長さ 1.750000、エントロピー 1.750000(第2節)。 第二に、偏った二記号では、最適な符号が大きく外れる──確率 0.99 でエントロピー 0.080793 ビットに対し、一記号ずつのハフマンは 1.000000 ビット(第3節)。 第三に、これが本稿の芯である。「最適な符号」がエントロピーの 12.377289 倍を使う──長さが整数でなければならず、一記号に 1 ビットより短い長さを割り当てられないからである(第3節)。 第四に、まとめると近づくが、上から近づくだけである──2 個・4 個・8 個ずつで 0.514950・0.272698・0.157158 ビット、差はいつも 1/k 未満(第3節)。 第五に、8 個ずつでも、まだ 1.945193 倍──クラフト和はどれも 1.000000 で、符号に隙間は無い(第3節)。 第六に、分離子は、各記号の確率が 2 の冪かである──冪なら一記号ずつで届き、冪でなければまとめる長さを伸ばしても差は消えきらない(第4節)。 ハフマン符号は最適だが、それは符号の長さが整数という縛りの中での最適である。確率が 1/2・1/4・1/8・1/8 なら平均の長さ 1.750000 はエントロピー 1.750000 にちょうど届く──長さが -log_2p_i そのものだからである。ところが片方の確率 0.99 の二記号では、エントロピー 0.080793 ビットに対し一記号ずつのハフマンは 1.000000 ビットで、エントロピーの 12.377289 倍を使う──一記号に 1 ビットより短い長さを割り当てられないからである。記号を 2 個・4 個・8 個ずつまとめると 0.514950・0.272698・0.157158 ビットに下がり、差はいつも 1/k 未満だが、8 個でもまだ 1.945193 倍が残る。分離子は、各記号の確率が 2 の冪かである──「ハフマンは最適か」は、何の中での最適かと確率の形を言うまで答が無い。既刊との位置──論文304 は通信路容量が有限では届かないことを示した。ここは情報源の側で、有限で届くかどうかが確率の形で決まる。論文163 の「これだ」の側に、条件つきの最適がある。正直に言えば──算術符号も記憶のある情報源も符号表の大きさも扱っていない。 作成にあたって:本稿の着想と内容は、著者自身の考察に基づくものです。文章の構成整理や英訳、数式の確認には AI(大規模言語モデル)の助力を得ました。最終的な内容の解釈や誤りがあれば、それらはすべて著者の責に帰します。お気づきの点があれば、ご教示いただければ幸いです。 キーワード:ハフマン符号、エントロピー、符号の長さ、クラフトの不等式、記号をまとめる符号化、整数の縛り。

title: Architecture d'un individu artificiel - v2 enrichie par la psychologie et la physiologie humaines.
abstract: This document describes, building block by building block, how one might design an "artificial individual": a machine that does more than answer questions, with a body, needs, emotions, memories, and a personality that develops over time. The architecture draws on current knowledge from human neuroscience, psychology, and physiology.What it coversThe document starts from an initial schema of 37 building blocks and examines it against research in neuroscience, psychology, and physiology. The resulting architecture contains 51 building blocks covering functions such as perception, bodily regulation, emotion, memory, decision-making, learning, sleep, and self-modeling.For each building block, the document describes what scientific research currently supports, the level of confidence in that knowledge, and how the underlying principle might be translated into a computational or robotic system.An appendix proposes an implementation plan consisting of 62 software modules, including their relationships, approximate operating timescales, and possible testing approaches.What it can be used for• Design: a starting map for researchers and engineers working on autonomous agents, embodied AI, or robotics.• Understanding: a structured overview of major functions performed by the human brain and body, decomposed into functional components for learning, teaching, or discussion.• Debate: an identification of potentially sensitive components, including pain, isolation, attachment, and other mechanisms that may raise ethical questions if implemented in artificial systems.• Sharing: the document is publicly timestamped and released for broad reuse. Its publication also creates a public record of the concepts and architectural elements described here, which may be relevant as prior art in future intellectual-property assessments.This is not a working system. It is an architectural and conceptual design proposal that has not yet been experimentally validated or peer reviewed.

title: Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic
abstract: In Sierra Leone, while artificial intelligence (AI) adoption remains limited to date, interest in identifying specific use cases is growing across government, academia, and the private sector. Governments everywhere are navigating uncharted waters as they seek to capitalize on AI’s rapidly evolving capabilities while designing safeguards to mitigate associated risks. This is taking place against the backdrop of a widening global AI divide. For Sierra Leone, strengthening the foundations for AI readiness will be critical to expanding the range of AI applications that the country can responsibly adopt, adapt, and sustain over time. As these foundations strengthen, AI can increasingly contribute to the country’s development objectives and improve outcomes for people, including through better public services and greater economic opportunities. At the same time, countries do not need to wait for all these foundations to be fully developed before beginning to benefit from AI. “Small AI” solutions—affordable and accessible systems designed to perform specific tasks under real-world resource constraints—offer a promising pathway for tackling development challenges in the near term, while investments in stronger foundations progressively expand what becomes possible. Realizing these opportunities will also require close partnership with the private sector, which is likely to play a central role in driving AI adoption and adaptation and in bringing AI-enabled services to businesses and households. This Report aims to support the government of Sierra Leone as it prepares a national AI strategy and works to accelerate digital transformation more broadly. The Report presents the results of a diagnostic exercise conducted in close partnership between the World Bank Group and Sierra Leone’s Ministry of Communications, Technology and Innovation. Through a combination of in-country stakeholder consultations and desk research, the Report assessed the strength of key AI enablers to identify gaps in the enabling environment and areas where AI can play a constructive role in achieving national development priorities. On this basis, the Report outlines short-, medium-, and long-term recommendations. To sequence and prioritize recommendations, the Report uses the Adopt, Adapt, Advance (3A) framework. Given the overall maturity of Sierra Leone’s digital ecosystem, the Report proposes focusing on a combination of the adoption pathway (which refers to the use of off-the-shelf AI tools and solutions) and, as digital foundations are strengthened, the adaptation pathway (which refers to customization of existing AI models to suit local contexts, languages, or use cases). The advancement pathway, which involves pretraining large, advanced models from scratch, building proprietary AI architectures, and conducting frontier AI research, is currently only feasible in a small number of countries given its reliance on frontier-scale compute and advanced research capabilities. AI readiness depends on the maturity of four foundations—Context, Connectivity, Compute, and Competency— that in turn require strong legal and institutional enablers for coordination and responsible AI governance (Figure A; collectively, the 4Cs+R Framework, with “R” referring to Responsible AI). The Report examines the current state of each of these core elements as a basis for the proposed recommendations. Instead of attempting to clearly distinguish between foundational needs for general digital transformation and AI-specific readiness, this Report uses the 3A lens to explain how the government’s vision for leveraging AI drives specific needs across these foundational 4Cs+R pillars.

evidence.title: Sierra Leone AI Readiness Diagnostic
evidence.abstract: In Sierra Leone, while artificial intelligence (AI) adoption remains limited to date, interest in identifying specific use cases is growing across government, academia, and the private sector. Governments everywhere are navigating uncharted waters as they seek to capitalize on AI’s rapidly evolving capabilities while designing safeguards to mitigate associated risks. This is taking place against the backdrop of a widening global AI divide. For Sierra Leone, strengthening the foundations for AI readiness will be critical to expanding the range of AI applications that the country can responsibly adopt, adapt, and sustain over time. As these foundations strengthen, AI can increasingly contribute to the country’s development objectives and improve outcomes for people, including through better public services and greater economic opportunities. At the same time, countries do not need to wait for all these foundations to be fully developed before beginning to benefit from AI. “Small AI” solutions—affordable and accessible systems designed to perform specific tasks under real-world resource constraints—offer a promising pathway for tackling development challenges in the near term, while investments in stronger foundations progressively expand what becomes possible. Realizing these opportunities will also require close partnership with the private sector, which is likely to play a central role in driving AI adoption and adaptation and in bringing AI-enabled services to businesses and households. This Report aims to support the government of Sierra Leone as it prepares a national AI strategy and works to accelerate digital transformation more broadly. The Report presents the results of a diagnostic exercise conducted in close partnership between the World Bank Group and Sierra Leone’s Ministry of Communications, Technology and Innovation. Through a combination of in-country stakeholder consultations and desk research, the Report assessed the strength of key AI enablers to identify gaps in the enabling environment and areas where AI can play a constructive role in achieving national development priorities. On this basis, the Report outlines short-, medium-, and long-term recommendations. To sequence and prioritize recommendations, the Report uses the Adopt, Adapt, Advance (3A) framework. Given the overall maturity of Sierra Leone’s digital ecosystem, the Report proposes focusing on a combination of the adoption pathway (which refers to the use of off-the-shelf AI tools and solutions) and, as digital foundations are strengthened, the adaptation pathway (which refers to customization of existing AI models to suit local contexts, languages, or use cases). The advancement pathway, which involves pretraining large, advanced models from scratch, building proprietary AI architectures, and conducting frontier AI research, is currently only feasible in a small number of countries given its reliance on frontier-scale compute and advanced research capabilities. AI readiness depends on the maturity of four foundations—Context, Connectivity, Compute, and Competency— that in turn require strong legal and institutional enablers for coordination and responsible AI governance (Figure A; collectively, the 4Cs+R Framework, with “R” referring to Responsible AI). The Report examines the current state of each of these core elements as a basis for the proposed recommendations. Instead of attempting to clearly distinguish between foundational needs for general digital transformation and AI-specific readiness, this Report uses the 3A lens to explain how the government’s vision for leveraging AI drives specific needs across these foundational 4Cs+R pillars.

title: Feature Drift‐Aware Boosted Ensemble (FDABE): A Dynamic Feature Weighting Framework for Concept Drift Adaptation in E‐Commerce Data Streams
abstract: ABSTRACT Concept drift is a central challenge in e‐commerce stream analytics because customer preferences and interaction patterns evolve over time. This paper proposes the Feature Drift‐Aware Boosted Ensemble (FDABE), which adapts at the feature level before updating the boosted learner. Its Feature Drift Severity Index (FDSI) combines Jensen‐Shannon distributional change, exponentially decayed drift memory, and temporal variation in feature relevance to drive dynamic feature influence and drift‐regularized boosting. On three public e‐commerce benchmarks, FDABE achieved 96.2% accuracy, 95.4% F1‐score, and 97.0% ROC‐AUC, with a 72‐sample detection delay and 148‐sample recovery time. A five‐seed confirmatory rerun across abrupt, gradual, incremental, recurring, subtle‐sparse, and noise‐obscured drift evaluated Precision, Recall, F1‐score, Balanced Accuracy, and PR‐AUC. FDABE significantly outperformed Static XGBoost, Incremental Weighted Ensemble, and Dynamic Ensemble Selection, while gains over Online Feature Screening were smaller. Differences versus Adaptive XGBoost, Evolving Gradient Boost, and JSD‐only Dynamic Feature Weighting were not significant after Holm correction. These results support FDABE as a competitive feature‐aware adaptation mechanism without claiming universal superiority.
